newsitem.title: UK: Zeneca to fight fungi with "green" product.
newsitem.headline: Zeneca to fight fungi with "green" product.

text.p: The outlook for rice blast, wheat yellow rust and other fungi damaging crops across the world is looking increasingly bleak as a unique, "green" agrochemical is set to take on all of them singlehandedly, developer Zeneca Group Plc claimed.
The British firm on Friday opened a 17.5 million pound ($29.4 million) factory in Scotland to produce 1500 tonnes per year of a fungicide called Amistar.
The product, which has its roots in a natural compound produced by mushrooms, could capture annual sales of over 300 million pounds in a three billion pound world market, analysts forecast.
"While it is unusual for an agrochemical to have such potential, Amistar could ultimately generate sales in excess of $500 million per annum," broker Merrill Lynch wrote a in report.

Zeneca, which currently has fungicide sales of $250 million, said Amistar is special because it can kill all types of diseases affecting cereals, fruit or vegetables. Only one or two fungi are able to resist it.
"It has a unique breadth of spectrum and high level of activity," Jeremy Godwin, a senior plant pathologist at Zeneca, told reporters.
Zeneca will try to compete with Amistar in about half of the world market after spending 14 years and about 60 million pounds on development.
Amistar is based on the organism strobilurin, which was discovered in former Czechoslovakia in the early 1970s and which helps woodland mushrooms compete with other fungi for nutrients.
Strobilurin makes other fungi starve from lack of energy. The problem with it is that it only works in darkness as it splits up in daylight.
To overcome this, Zeneca synthesised over 1400 compounds before discovering Amistar, which works as strobilurin, but is more stable and therefore more effective.
The product nevertheless still dissolves relatively fast with sunlight breaking it up in simple molecules, Zeneca said.
"We have a product that works, that has an awesome spectrum and that is safe," said David Evans, development director at Zeneca Agrochemicals.

Rival BASF from Germany has developed a product which works along the same principle as Amistar, but which has to be mixed with existing products to kill as many fungi simultaneously as Amistar does on its own, Zeneca officials said.
"It is in the same class of chemistry, but a different chemical," said Vivienne Anthony, Zeneca's fungicides development manager. "It (Amistar) has a broader spectrum."
Zeneca has already sold small quantities of Amistar in Germany and Ireland in the spring of 1996.
It wants to raise sales next year after having been granted approval for marketing in another five countries. These are South Africa and and four Latin American countries.
Regulatory approval in Britain and the U.S. is expected soon. ($1=.5950 Pound)
